lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Frames and structures are the skeleton of any metal furniture. Whether you are making a chair, a table, a bed, or a gate, the frame carries the load and keeps everything square and stable. In Africa, where furniture often has to withstand heavy use, rough surfaces, and sometimes outdoor conditions, a strong frame is not optionalâit is the difference between a product that lasts for years and one that collapses in months. Think about the metal beds common in many homes: if the frame is weak, the bed sags and squeaks. A well-built frame, on the other hand, can support a family and be passed down.

Why does this matter for your business? Customers talk. If you sell a wobbly table, word spreads fast. But if your furniture is rock-solid, you get repeat orders and referrals. Good frames also allow you to use less materialâif you design smart, you can make a strong frame with thinner tubing, saving money on steel. That is profit in your pocket.

In this module, you will learn the basics of frame construction: how to measure, cut, join, and brace metal to create structures that do not twist or collapse. We focus on practical methods using common tools like angle grinders, welding machines, and measuring tapes. You will learn to work with square and rectangular tubing, round pipes, and angle ironâmaterials easily found in local markets or scrap yards.

By the end of this module, you will be able to build a simple stool or small table frame from start to finish. You will know how to check for square, how to weld joints that hold, and how to avoid common mistakes that lead to weak furniture. This skill is the foundation for every other metal furniture project you will ever do. So letâs get startedâyour ability to build strong frames will set you apart as a craftsman.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To build metal frames, you need a basic set of tools and the right materials. You do not need a fully equipped workshop to startâmany successful metalworkers begin with just a few key tools. Here is what you need: a measuring tape (5m is fine), a carpenterâs square or engineerâs square, a scriber or marker, an angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs, a welding machine (arc welder is common and affordable), welding rods (2.5mm or 3.2mm), a hammer, a wire brush, and safety gear (goggles, gloves, apron, and boots). A magnetic welding square is also very helpful for holding joints at 90 degrees. If you donât have a welder yet, you can start with bolted joints, but welding is stronger and faster.

For materials, the most common are mild steel tubes: square tubing (e.g., 25mm x 25mm x 1.5mm wall thickness), rectangular tubing (e.g., 40mm x 20mm), and round pipe (e.g., 25mm diameter). Angle iron (e.g., 25mm x 25mm x 3mm) is also useful for legs and supports. You can buy new steel from hardware stores or steel merchants, but many African craftsmen save money by using recycled steel from scrap yardsâold bed frames, car parts, and gates can be cut and reused. Just make sure the metal is clean and not badly rusted. For outdoor furniture, consider galvanized steel or apply anti-rust paint.

You will also need consumables: cutting discs, grinding discs, welding rods, and paint or oil to protect the finished frame. A good workbench or sturdy table is essentialâyou can make one from wood or metal. A vice is useful for holding pieces while cutting or welding. Finally, a fire extinguisher or bucket of sand should be nearby when welding, as sparks can start fires.

Start with the basics: a grinder, a welder, a square, and a tape. As you earn, add more tools like a chop saw (for accurate cuts) or a magnetic drill. Remember, quality tools save time and produce better work. Buy the best you can afford, and maintain themâclean your welder, change discs when worn, and keep your square accurate.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Building a metal frame follows a clear sequence. We will use a simple stool frame as an example: a square top (350mm x 350mm) with four legs (450mm high). First, plan and measure. Draw a simple sketch with dimensions. For the top, cut four pieces of 25mm square tubing to 350mm each. For the legs, cut four pieces to 450mm. Use an angle grinder with a cutting disc. Make sure cuts are squareâcheck with a square. Deburr the ends with a grinding disc.

Second, lay out the top frame on a flat surface. Arrange the four pieces into a square, with the ends meeting at 90 degrees. Use a carpenterâs square to check corners. Clamp or tack weld the corners. Tack welding means making small welds at each joint to hold everything in place. Check for square by measuring diagonalsâthey must be equal. If not, adjust and re-tack. Once square, weld all around each joint. Grind the welds smooth if desired.

Third, attach the legs. Turn the top frame upside down. Place a leg at each corner, ensuring it is flush with the outside edges. Use a square to make sure the leg is perpendicular to the top. Tack weld each leg in two places (opposite sides). Check that all legs are vertical and the frame does not wobble. Measure from the bottom of one leg to the bottom of the opposite leg diagonallyâboth diagonals should be equal. If not, adjust. Then weld all around each leg joint.

Fourth, add braces for strength. For a stool, you can add a brace between legs about 100mm from the bottom. Cut two pieces of tubing to fit between the legs (front-back and side-side). Weld them in place. This prevents the legs from splaying out. Finally, clean the frame: grind welds, brush off slag, and wipe with a cloth. Apply a coat of red oxide primer, then paint your chosen colour. Let it dry. Your stool frame is complete and ready for a seat (wood, metal, or woven).

Remember: measure twice, cut once. Tack weld, check, then fully weld. Always work on a flat surface. With practice, you can build a frame like this in under two hours.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Even experienced welders make mistakes. Here are common problems when building frames and how to fix them. Mistake 1: Frame is not square. This happens when you donât check diagonals or weld too quickly. Fix: Before fully welding, measure diagonals. If unequal, use a clamp or hammer to adjust until equal, then re-tack. Always tack weld first, check, then weld fully. Mistake 2: Legs are not perpendicular. If legs lean, the furniture will wobble. Fix: Use a square against the top and leg. Tack weld, check with a plumb line or square, adjust, then weld. Mistake 3: Weak welds. This occurs if the metal is dirty, the current is too low, or you move too fast. Fix: Clean metal with a grinder before welding. Set welder to correct amperage (e.g., 90-120 amps for 2.5mm rods on 3mm steel). Practice on scrap. Make sure you penetrate the joint. Mistake 4: Distortion. Welding heats metal, causing it to bend. Fix: Weld small sections at a time, alternating sides. Clamp pieces to a flat surface. Allow to cool between welds. Mistake 5: Porous welds (holes). This is from moisture or rust. Fix: Use dry rods, clean metal, and proper technique. Mistake 6: Sharp edges. Grind all cut ends and welds smooth to avoid injuries and improve appearance. Mistake 7: No bracing. Without braces, frames twist. Fix: Add diagonal or horizontal braces. For a table, add a brace between legs. Mistake 8: Using wrong material thickness. Too thin and it bends; too thick and itâs heavy and expensive. Fix: For furniture, 1.5mm to 2mm wall thickness is good for most applications. Mistake 9: Not checking level. If the floor is uneven, your frame might rock. Fix: After building, place on a flat surface and adjust legs by grinding or adding shims. Mistake 10: Skipping safety. Always wear PPE. Fix: Put on goggles, gloves, and apron before starting. These mistakes are easy to avoid with patience and careful checking. Remember: a few extra minutes checking saves hours of rework.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety is not optional in metalwork. Every year, craftsmen are injured because they skip basic precautions. You must protect your eyes, lungs, skin, and ears. Always wear safety goggles when cutting or grindingâsparks and metal shards can blind you. Wear a welding helmet or face shield when welding. Use earplugs or earmuffs when grinding, as the noise can damage hearing. Wear leather gloves to protect hands from cuts and burns. A leather apron or heavy cotton overalls protect your body from sparks and hot metal. Steel-toe boots protect your feet from falling metal. Never wear loose clothing or open shoes.

Ventilation is critical. Welding fumes are toxic. Work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. If indoors, use a fan to blow fumes away, but not directly on the weld (it can disrupt shielding gas if using MIG). Keep a fire extinguisher or bucket of sand nearby. Never weld near flammable materials like paint, petrol, or wood. Check for fire hazards after weldingâsparks can smoulder for hours. Use a fire blanket or wet cloth to cool hot metal before touching.

Best practices for quality and efficiency: Plan your work. Measure twice, cut once. Keep your work area clean and organized. Store tools safely. Maintain your equipment: change grinder discs when worn, check welding cables for damage, and keep your welder dry. Use jigs or fixtures for repeated partsâthis ensures consistency. When welding, use the correct amperage and rod size. For 3mm steel, use 2.5mm rod at 90-110 amps. For thinner metal, use lower amps. Practice on scrap to dial in settings. Always tack weld before full welding. Check square and level at every stage. Grind welds for a clean finish. Apply anti-rust primer and paint to protect your work. Finally, take breaks. Fatigue leads to mistakes and injuries. Drink water. Stretch. A fresh mind works better. By following these safety rules and best practices, you will build strong, safe furniture and build a reputation as a reliable craftsman.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now itâs time to put your skills to work. In this exercise, you will build a simple metal stool frame. This project uses the techniques from this module: measuring, cutting, squaring, tack welding, and bracing. You will need: 25mm square tubing (about 2.5 meters total), angle grinder, welding machine, 2.5mm welding rods, square, measuring tape, scriber, hammer, wire brush, and safety gear. Optional: magnetic square, clamps.

Step 1: Cut the pieces. You need four pieces of 350mm for the top frame, four pieces of 450mm for the legs, and two pieces of 250mm for braces (these will be cut to fit later). Use your grinder to cut. Deburr all ends.

Step 2: Build the top frame. Lay the four 350mm pieces on a flat surface to form a square. Check corners with a square. Tack weld each corner. Measure diagonalsâthey must be equal. Adjust if needed. Then weld all around each corner. Grind smooth.

Step 3: Attach legs. Turn the top frame upside down. Place a leg at each corner, flush with the outside. Use a square to ensure each leg is perpendicular. Tack weld each leg in two opposite spots. Check that all legs are vertical and the frame sits flat. Measure diagonals from leg bottomsâthey must be equal. Adjust if needed. Weld all around each leg joint. Grind smooth.

Step 4: Add braces. Measure the distance between the front legs at about 100mm from the bottom. Cut a piece of tubing to fit. Weld it between the legs. Repeat for the side braces. These braces prevent the legs from spreading. Ensure they are level.

Step 5: Clean and finish. Grind all welds smooth. Brush off slag. Wipe with a cloth. Apply a coat of red oxide primer. Let dry. Then paint with your chosen colour (e.g., black, red, or green). Let dry completely.

Step 6: Test. Place the stool on a flat floor. It should not wobble. Sit on it (carefully) to test strength. If it holds, you have succeeded. If not, check for weak welds or missing braces. Take a photo of your finished frameâthis is your portfolio piece. With this stool, you have mastered the basics of frame construction. Now you can scale up to tables, beds, and more. Practice makes perfectâbuild at least three stools to perfect your technique.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a frame in metal furniture?
options: B) To carry the load and keep the structure stable
C) To reduce the weight of the furniture
quiz.explanation: The frame provides structural support and stability.

quiz.q: Which of these is a common material for metal furniture frames?
quiz.explanation: Square steel tubing is widely used for its strength and availability.

quiz.q: Why is it important to build strong frames for furniture in Africa?
options: B) Because furniture must withstand heavy use and rough conditions
C) Because there are no other materials
D) Because customers prefer weak furniture
quiz.explanation: African furniture often faces heavy use and environmental challenges, requiring robust construction.

quiz.q: What tool is used to check if a corner is 90 degrees?
quiz.explanation: A carpenter's square is used to check right angles.

quiz.q: Which welding rod size is commonly used for 3mm steel?
quiz.explanation: 2.5mm rods are suitable for 3mm steel at around 90-110 amps.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a magnetic welding square?
options: B) To hold joints at 90 degrees
quiz.explanation: It holds metal pieces at right angles during tack welding.

quiz.q: What does 'tack weld' mean?
options: A) A small weld to hold pieces in place
B) A full weld around a joint
C) A type of welding rod
quiz.explanation: Tack welds are temporary small welds used to secure alignment before final welding.

quiz.q: How can you check if a rectangular frame is square?
options: A) Measure the length of all sides
B) Measure the diagonals; they should be equal
D) Weld it and see if it wobbles
quiz.explanation: Equal diagonals indicate a square frame.

quiz.q: What should you do before fully welding a frame?
options: B) Tack weld and check for square
quiz.explanation: Tack welding allows you to check and adjust alignment before final welding.

quiz.q: Why are braces added to a stool frame?
options: B) To prevent legs from splaying out
quiz.explanation: Braces add rigidity and prevent legs from spreading under load.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of weak welds?
options: A) Using too much welding rod
B) Dirty metal or low amperage
quiz.explanation: Dirty metal and incorrect amperage lead to poor penetration and weak welds.

quiz.q: How can you reduce distortion when welding a frame?
options: B) Weld small sections and alternate sides
C) Use a bigger welding rod
quiz.explanation: Alternating welds and allowing cooling reduces heat buildup and distortion.

quiz.q: What should you do if a leg is not perpendicular to the top frame?
options: A) Leave it; it will be fine
B) Adjust and re-tack before final welding
quiz.explanation: Correcting alignment before final welding ensures a stable frame.

quiz.q: Why is it important to deburr cut metal ends?
options: A) To make them look shiny
B) To prevent injuries and improve weld quality
quiz.explanation: Deburring removes sharp edges and prepares the surface for welding.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a recommended safety gear for welding?
quiz.explanation: Open-toe sandals do not protect feet from sparks or falling metal.

quiz.q: What is the correct amperage range for welding 3mm steel with a 2.5mm rod?
quiz.explanation: 90-110 amps is typical for 2.5mm rods on 3mm steel.

quiz.q: Why should you work in a well-ventilated area when welding?
options: D) To prevent metal from rusting
quiz.explanation: Welding fumes are hazardous; ventilation disperses them.

quiz.q: What should be kept nearby in case of fire when welding?
options: B) A fire extinguisher or bucket of sand
quiz.explanation: Fire extinguisher or sand can quickly put out small fires caused by sparks.

quiz.q: What is the recommended wall thickness for furniture steel tubing?
quiz.explanation: 1.5mm to 2mm provides a good balance of strength and weight.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid welding near flammable materials?
quiz.explanation: Welding sparks can easily start fires with flammable materials.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a metal frame?
quiz.explanation: Planning and measuring ensure accurate cuts and a successful build.

quiz.q: When building the stool frame in the practical exercise, what is the length of the top frame pieces?
quiz.explanation: The top frame pieces are cut to 350mm each.

quiz.q: How many legs does the stool frame have?
quiz.explanation: The stool has four legs, one at each corner.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of applying red oxide primer?
quiz.explanation: Red oxide primer protects steel from rust before painting.

quiz.q: What should you do after welding to ensure a clean finish?
options: B) Grind welds and brush off slag
quiz.explanation: Grinding and brushing remove slag and create a smooth surface.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check the level of a finished frame?
options: A) To ensure it doesn't wobble
B) To make it look good
quiz.explanation: A level frame sits flat and stable on the floor.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when cutting metal tubing?
quiz.explanation: Inaccurate measurement leads to ill-fitting joints and wasted material.

quiz.q: How can you prevent legs from splaying out on a stool?
options: A) Weld them at an angle
quiz.explanation: Braces connect legs and prevent outward movement.

quiz.q: What is the recommended way to hold pieces for welding?
options: B) With clamps or magnetic squares
quiz.explanation: Clamps or magnetic squares securely hold pieces at correct angles.

quiz.q: Why should you take breaks when welding for long periods?
options: B) To avoid fatigue and mistakes
C) To let the welder cool
quiz.explanation: Fatigue reduces focus and increases the risk of errors and injuries.
